'''''Drimys winteri''''', also known as '''Winter's bark''', '''foye'''<ref name="M">{{cite book|last=de Mösbach|first=Ernesto Wilhelm|date=1992|title=Botánica indígena de Chile|language=es|location=Santiago, Chile|publisher=Editorial Andrés Bello|pages=78–79|isbn=956-13-0970-X}}</ref> and '''canelo''', is a slender species of tree in the [[family (botany)|family]] Winteraceae, growing up to {{convert|20|m|0|abbr=on}} tall. It is native to the [[Magellanic subpolar forests|Magellanic]] and [[Valdivian temperate forests]] of Chile and Argentina, where it is a dominant tree in the coastal evergreen forests. It is found below {{convert|1200|m|abbr=on}} between latitude [[32nd parallel south|32° south]] and Cape Horn at [[56th parallel south|latitude 56°]]. In its southernmost natural range it can tolerate temperatures down to {{convert|-20|C|F|abbr=on}}.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Angiosperms (Flowering Plants) |url=https://www.earth.com/plant-encyclopedia/angiosperms/ |access-date=2023-10-19 |website=Earth.com |language=en}}</ref> The plant is renowned for its [[phenotypic plasticity]] being able to grow in different sites from "extreme [[arid]] zones to [[wetland]]s along Chile".<ref name=flood2017>{{Cite journal|title=Which seed origin provides better tolerance to flooding and drought when restoring to face climate change?|journal=[[Austral Ecology]]|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/320384888|last1=Bustos-Salazar|first1=Angela|last2=Smith-Ramírez|first2=Cecilia|doi=10.1111/aec.12521|year=2017|last3=Zúñiga-Feest|first3=Alejandra|last4=Alves|first4=Fernanda|last5=Ivanovich|first5=Rodrigo|volume=42|issue=8|pages=934–946|bibcode=2017AusEc..42..934B }}</ref><ref name=Bosque2020-3/> The tree does also grow in places with various types and degrees of [[Competition (biology)|competition from other plants]].<ref name=Bosque2020-3>{{Cite journal|title=Modelos de efectos mixtos de altura-diámetro para Drimys winteri en el sur (41-43° S) de Chile|journal=[[Bosque (journal)|Bosque]]|url=https://scielo.conicyt.cl/scielo.php?pid=S0717-92002019000100071&script=sci_arttext|trans-title=Mixed-effects height-diameter models for Drimys winteri in the south (41-43° S) of Chile |last1=Salas-Eljatib|first1=Christian|volume=40|last2=Cordvalán|first2=Patricio|last3=Pino|first3=Nicolás|last4=Donoso|first4=Pablo J.|last5=Soto|first5=Daniel P.|publisher=[[Austral University of Chile]]|issue=1|doi=10.4067/S0717-92002019000100071  |language=Spanish |year=2019|pages=71–80|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Description==
The leaves are [[Glossary of leaf morphology|lanceolate]], glossy green above, whitish below and can measure up to {{convert|20|cm|0|abbr=on}}. The flowers are white with a yellow center, and consist of a great number of petals and [[stamen]]s. The fruit is a bluish [[Berry (botany)|berry]].

The [[Tree height measurement|height]]–[[Diameter at breast height|diameter]] relation of ''D. winteri'' varies greatly. There is for example more spread in ''D. winteri'' height–diameter relations than for ''[[Nothofagus]]'' species.<ref name=Bosque2020-3/> Part of the spread can be explained as reflecting higher tree density that correlates with larger heights for a given diameter.<ref name=Bosque2020-3/>{{clarify|date=January 2023}} Within its range ''D. winteri'' is more [[frost resistance|frost-tolerant]] than naturally occurring [[conifers]] and vessel-bearing [[Flowering plant|angiosperms]] such as the ''Nothofagus''.<ref name=nvessel2002>{{Cite journal|title=Hardly a relict: Freezing and the evolution of vesselless wood in Winteraceae|journal=[[Evolution (journal)|Evolution]]|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1111/j.0014-3820.2002.tb01359.x|last1=Feild|first1=Taylor S.|volume=56|pages=464–478|last2=Brodribb|first2=Tim|issue=3|year=2002|last3=Holbrook|first3=N. Michele|doi=10.1111/j.0014-3820.2002.tb01359.x|pmid=11989678|bibcode=2002Evolu..56..464F |s2cid=31376453 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> This challenged conventional views  that plants without [[Vessel element|vessels]] such as ''D. winteri'' would be [[relict (biology)|biological relicts]] poorly adapted to cold.<ref name=nvessel2002/>

==History==
The canelo or foye is the [[sacred tree]] of the [[Mapuche]], who associated it with "good, peace and justice",<ref name=Sonia2015>{{Cite book|title=Mitos de Chile: Enciclopedia de seres, apariciones y encantos|last=Montecino Aguirre|first=Sonia|publisher=[[Catalonia (publisher)|Catalonia]] |year=2015|isbn=978-956-324-375-8 |pages=126–127|chapter=Canelo |language=es}}</ref> often planted in special gatherings. Priests of their [[Mapuche religion|native religion]] were named ''foyeweye'' or ''boquibuye'', "servant of the ''foye''".<ref name="M"/>

When [[Sir Francis Drake]] sailed [[Francis Drake's Circumnavigation|round the world in 1577-80]], of the four ships accompanying the ''[[Golden Hind]]'' at the outset, the only ship that successfully reached the entrance to the [[Strait of Magellan]] was the ''Elizabeth'', captained by [[John Wynter]].  Before entering the Strait, in July 1578, Drake sent Wynter ashore where he learned indigenous people ate the astringent bark.<ref>{{cite book | title=Two Voyages to the Pacific Coast of North America: Francis Drake and Brune de Hezeta, Their Voyages Compared with Information about Scurvy | first1=Robert G. | last1 = Lynch | first2=Samuel | last2=Spivak | publisher=Drake Navigators Guild | location=San Francisco | date=2017 | page =37}}</ref>  The ''Elizabeth'' transversed the Strait.  A week later the two ships were  separated in a storm and Wynter turned back.  Wynter returned in 1580<ref>{{cite book|last=Coote |first=Stephen |date=2005 |title=Drake: The Life and Legend of an Elizabethan Hero |location=New York |publisher=Thomas Dunne Books |isbn=978-0-7434-6870-1}}</ref> with a supply of ''Drimys'' bark, and for centuries before [[vitamin C]] was isolated, "Winter's Bark" was esteemed as a preventive and remedy for [[scurvy]]— correctly so, for an [[infusion]] of ''D. winteri'' sustained [[James Cook|Captain James Cook]] and his crew in the South Pacific, and the naturalist accompanying his voyage of exploration, [[Johann Reinhold Forster]], was the first to officially describe and name ''D. winteri''.<ref>Alice M. Coats, ''Garden Shrubs and Their Histories'' (1964) 1992, ''s.v.'' "Drimys".</ref>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Rewe ñadi mew.JPG|thumb|180px|right|A [[rehue|rewe]] and canelo tree in the [[Austral University of Chile]].]]
[[File:Canelo_(Drimys_winteri)_fruits_(Inao_Vásquez).jpg|180px|right|fruits]]
''Drimys winteri'' is grown in cool moist climates<ref>John L. Creech, providing American garden notes for Coats 1992, remarks of ''D. winteri'' and [[Tasmania]]n ''D. aromatica'', both grown in British gardens, "These two species have not had much success here"; ''Drimys winteri'' is grown in the [http://www.sfbotanicalgarden.org/Gardens/bloom_06_12.shtml San Francisco Botanical Garden] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120309142206/http://www.sfbotanicalgarden.org/Gardens/bloom_06_12.shtml |date=2012-03-09 }}: (Capt. Winter is identified as "William Winter").</ref> as an [[ornamental plant]] for its red-brown bark, bright green fragrant leaves and its clusters of creamy white [[jasmine]]-scented flowers.

The species grows well in southern [[Great Britain]], flourishing as far north as [[Anglesey]]. Specimens brought from the southern forests of [[Tierra del Fuego]] and planted in the [[Faroe Islands]] have proven to be especially hardy.<ref>Højgaard, A., J. Jóhansen, and S. Ødum (eds) 1989.'' A century of tree planting in the Faroe Islands''. Føroya Frodskaparfelag, Torshavn.</ref>

This plant has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=''Drimys winteri''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/31925/Drimys-winteri/Details|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|access-date=1 June 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 33 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 6 February 2018}}</ref>

It has been planted in the North Pacific Coast of the United States.<ref name=Seattle.gov>{{cite web|url=http://www.seattle.gov/parks/proparks/projects/ArboretumReport.pdf |title=''Drimys winteri'' in Washington Park Arboretum |publisher=Seattle Government |access-date=2009-06-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090324233535/http://www.seattle.gov/parks/proparks/projects/ArboretumReport.pdf |archive-date=2009-03-24 }}</ref>

The species is considered to have a potential for [[flood]] mitigation in [[Norte Chico, Chile|northern Chile]] if planted in valleys.<ref name=flood2017/>

==Other uses==
Canelo wood is reddish in color and heavy, with a very beautiful grain. It is used for furniture and musical instruments. The wood is not durable outdoors because continuous rainfalls damage it. The wood is not good for making bonfires because it gives off a spicy smoke.

The bark is gray, thick and soft and is used as a pepper replacement in Argentina and Chile. The peppery compound in canelo is [[polygodial]].<ref>Muñoz-Concha, D., Vogel, H., Yunesc, R., Razmilic, I., Brescianic, L., and Malheiros, A., Presence of polygodial and drimenol in Drimys populations from Chile, ''Biochemical Systematics and Ecology'', Volume 35, Issue 7, July 2007, Pages 434-438</ref>

''D. winteri'' is an [[insect repellent]] and [[fumigant]].<ref name="Zapata-Smagghe-2010-bundle">
